I've seen one too many of these things today. "Scientific and magical [some number under 10] minute bodyweight workout for getting ripped easy and quick", or "666 pushups a day for unholy Satanic gains". Well, they don't work, and since it gets tiring explaining why they don't work almost daily, I'm writing this article both as an educational piece, and as a reference point, something to point people to in these situations.

First of all, those seven-minute workouts you see are something called "circuit training", which is cardio. And not good cardio. The two most important things for cardio are that it burns calories, and doesn't interfere with your strength training. Seven minute workouts comprised of high repetition pushups, bodyweight squats, and "mountain climbers" fulfills neither of those criteria. For better cardio, without equipment, try going for a run, or even a brisk walk. It burns more calories, and it fucks with your recovery much, much less.

Oh yeah, strength training, I almost forgot. That is what your bodyweight workouts are actually supposed to be. And if they are to be strength training, they have to utilize a little something called "progression". And if they are to be progressive, and you are to make progress, then they can't be the same every time you do them, capisce? That's another point where those things fail.

And while we're on the subject of progress, it's important to point out that the kind of progress we're aiming to make is strength progress. This is why those programs that have you do increasing numbers of pushups ad infinitum don't work. Sure you've made progress, in your ability to do tons of pushups, anyways. But the progress isn't meaningful, because you didn't get stronger, and you didn't build muscle [don't let the pump fool you]. You just became more efficient at doing more pushups.

Making strength progress over endurance progress is important for two reasons. One, strength carries over into everything you do, whereas endurance is very much specific to the thing you built it doing. Two, strength progress builds muscle, whereas endurance progress really only builds neurological efficiency at that specific movement. This is due to something called Henneman's size principle, which basically states that your body only engages all of it's muscle fibers under high load, and only recruits a minimal amount of smaller and harder to fatigue muscle fibers under low load. This is why a fairly small amount of strength training can build muscle, but all the cardio in the world never will.

And thus, the most important thing for strength progress is keeping your reps low [think less than 8], and the relative load high, and to do this without external weight, you must progress to harder and harder movements as you become stronger. This is where movement progression chains come into play [noticing a trend here yet?]. When pushups get too easy, you place your hands closer together, then elevate your feet, then begin focusing on one arm at a time, and them doing pushups with only one arm at a time. It's all about leverage and mechanical disadvantage. Eventually you are strong enough to go through the same motion with one arm that you used to do with two, how crazy is that?

Anyways, I hope this has been educational for you inexperienced in the art of bodyweight strength training. It will certainly be useful to me from now on, when I inevitably see more of those terrible, blasphemous workouts [probably created by fat chicks on tumblr] inevitably being posted here and everywhere else. I invite you to use it for that purpose too.

Also, please upvote this so people can see it while it's fresh and new. The more who know these basics, the less can fall for the idiocy. Thanks, friend.
